comparator.name: International Bachelor Arts and Culture Studies
comparator.route: Culture and Economics focus area with minor
comparator.sourceNotes: Reconstructed from the official 2026-2027 ESHCC Teaching and Examination Regulations, corroborated by the current programme and programme-overview pages. The 180-EC pathway contains 60 EC of first-year mandatory study; 35 EC of later theoretical core; 10 EC of later methods; three 5-EC focus-area courses; one 5-EC research workshop; a 15-EC internship; a 15-EC individual Bachelor Graduation Project; one 5-EC year-two elective; and a third-year option comprising a 15-EC minor, two of the three required focus-area courses and a second 5-EC elective. The two year-three focus courses are therefore counted once within the 15-EC focus-area total, not again as extra credits. The generic target does not choose among three formal focus areas. Culture and Economics is selected because it is listed first. Its first three officially listed courses are instantiated, and Management of Arts and Culture is its sole listed research workshop. The first-listed minor route is selected over exchange, while the minor and elective subjects remain generic rather than invented.

alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Compared with the closest programme, this route removes business, organisational leadership, marketing, market research, advanced microeconomics, media archaeology, race/media, literature foundations, art-historical writing and public rhetoric. It adds law, human rights, philosophy, ethics, EU politics, peace and conflict, environmental justice and a four-course History strand. Thirteen courses are shared and eleven differ. The organising choice moves from a broad arts-and-cultural-sector curriculum to culture's relationship with institutions, collective life, conflict, inequality and public challenges.

comparatorRouteSelection.route: Culture and Economics focus area with minor
comparatorRouteSelection.basis: The normalized target is the generic IBACS bachelor. The current official curriculum gives no academic basis for preferring Culture and Economics, Culture and Society or Culture and Media as more representative of the programme as a whole. Culture and Economics is listed first, its first three listed courses are instantiated, and the minor route is listed before exchange. These choices follow official order before and independently of UCR course selection.

candidateAssessments.organisingLogic: The explicitly supplied candidate direction is “Culture, society and societal challenges”; its interest-row basis and disposition remain explicit in interestSelection.
candidateAssessments.assessment: The academic decision includes this candidate as ucr-2.

candidateAssessments.organisingLogic: The explicitly supplied candidate direction is “Culture, media and digital change”; its interest-row basis and disposition remain explicit in interestSelection.

progressionAssessment.rationale: Business, economics, sociology and Western art history establish the organisational, economic, social and visual foundations in semester 1. Research Methods & Statistics precedes every selected course that formally requires it. Introductory sociology and art history precede modern sociology, advanced social theory and advanced museum and heritage work; Introduction to Film & Media precedes Media & Race. The final year consolidates cultural theory, media history and representation, literature, market research, art-historical writing and public rhetoric. Every course is available in its assigned term and every formal prerequisite is completed in an earlier semester.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The closest programme integrates art and cultural history, heritage, sociology, economics, organisations, policy, media, literature and research. Two further generator-backed directions remain coherent and feasible: Culture and Society organises the societal-challenge interests around sociology, history, heritage, institutions, ethics and collective action, while Culture and Media organises globalisation and digitalisation around media theory, communication, audiences, representation, platform change and creative production. The routes share 13 courses between the closest and society routes, 12 between the closest and media routes, and 6 between the society and media routes. Each pair clears the 4-course floor and expresses a different academic organising logic. The maximum of three alternatives is reached.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both provide a chronological foundation in Western art and culture; UCR concentrates on visual art and does not cover literature, architecture and music to the same extent.
Both treat heritage as culturally produced and interpreted; UCR approaches this through global archaeology and material culture rather than contemporary heritage institutions alone.
Both develop independent, evidence-based research and writing in arts and culture; the comparator requires a larger 15-EC individual graduation project.
The comparator applies economics specifically to cultural heritage. UCR offers heritage and economics in separate courses but no scheduled course combining them directly.
The comparator contains a dedicated history of the art market. UCR covers art history and economic markets separately but does not force a weaker one-course equivalence.
Both introduce sociological concepts and perspectives for understanding cultural production and social life; the comparator applies them specifically to arts and culture.
Both critically examine modernity, social theory and ideas of progress; UCR gives additional attention to imperialism and colonial responses.
Both develop advanced contemporary social theory and apply it to institutions and civil society; the comparator remains specifically centred on cultural sociology.
Both examine public institutions and policy decision-making; the comparator specialises in government intervention for culture, while UCR focuses on EU governance.
Both introduce microeconomic and macroeconomic concepts; the comparator applies them directly to cultural and creative markets.
Both analyse choices by producers and consumers, market structure and economic evidence; the comparator is specifically cultural economics.
Both use economic theory and evidence to evaluate policy and industry developments; UCR emphasises public economics rather than one cultural industry.
Both use applied project work to examine how organisations develop ideas, models and strategies; the comparator workshop is specific to arts management.
Both examine organisational structures, leadership, culture and performance; the comparator focuses on cultural and creative organisations.
Both examine audiences, engagement and marketing strategy; UCR teaches general responsible marketing rather than arts marketing alone.
Both assess technological change, innovation, risks and future strategies; UCR approaches these through responsible digital transformation across organisations.
The comparator includes a dedicated course on creativity, cities and cultural geography. No scheduled UCR course provides that same geographic specialisation.
Both introduce relations among arts, culture, media, representation and cultural production, including how media reshape identities and power.
Both introduce social-science research design and evaluation; UCR also includes experimental and survey methods with descriptive and inferential statistics.
Both develop practical quantitative-data skills; UCR emphasises data cleaning and visualisation across disciplines rather than SPSS-based statistical analysis.
Both teach hands-on qualitative design, data collection, interpretation and reflexive social research.
Both develop critical reading, writing, presentation and academic practice; UCR additionally foregrounds personal, ethical and professional development.
The comparator requires a 15-EC field-specific arts-and-culture internship. None of the scheduled UCR courses is a workplace placement.
The comparator includes a 15-EC approved minor. UCR breadth and choice are distributed across the complete liberal-arts curriculum rather than represented by one scheduled course.
The comparator retains a 5-EC open elective in year 2. UCR elective choice is distributed across each 180-EC pathway, so no single scheduled course is asserted as its equivalent.
The selected minor route retains a second 5-EC open elective in year 3. UCR elective choice is distributed across each 180-EC pathway, so no single scheduled course is asserted as its equivalent.

notes.text: IBACS is a continuous interdisciplinary Arts and Culture Studies degree with dedicated cultural sociology, cultural economics, cultural policy, arts marketing, cultural management, heritage, focus-area study, a research workshop, a compulsory arts-and-culture internship and a 15-EC individual graduation project. UCR can build strong pathways across art history, heritage, sociology, economics, organisations, media, communication and research, but it does not reproduce that complete specialist sequence or mandatory professional placement.
